title: Talking about more than one
goal: Form Norwegian plurals with one ending that covers most words — then recognize the handful of common words that break the rule.
bekal: form plurals with **-er** and definite plurals with **-ene**
know why *et hus* doesn't change in the plural but *et vindu* does
name family members and ask how many with *hvor mange*
wave: Go back over **Unit 3** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Test yourself on one point only — where does the verb stand?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Familien
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon in the common room. Ingrid is folding laundry, Budi is waiting for the water to boil.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.id: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, jeg har to brødre og ei søster.
lines.id: Yes, I have two brothers and a sister.
lines.literal: yes, I have two brothers and a sister.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Så mange! Jeg har bare én bror.
lines.id: So many! I only have one brother.
lines.literal: so many! I have only one brother.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do your parents live in Bergen?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nei, de bor på en gård utenfor byen.
lines.id: No, they live on a farm outside the city.
lines.literal: no, they live on a farm outside the-city.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A farm? Do they have animals?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Fire hester, to hunder og altfor mange katter.
lines.id: Four horses, two dogs and far too many cats.
lines.literal: four horses, two dogs and all-too many cats.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ingen vet. Katta får barn hvert år.
lines.id: Nobody knows. The cat has kittens every year.
lines.literal: nobody knows. the-cat gets children every year.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ja, men jeg liker mennesker bedre. Dyr snakker ikke norsk.
lines.id: Yes, but I like people better. Animals don't speak Norwegian.
lines.literal: yes, but I like people better. animals speak not Norwegian.

notes: **There's just one main rule:** add **-er** for the plural and **-ene** for the definite plural. *en katt → katter → kattene*. About eight out of ten nouns follow this pattern without argument.

**Brødre and søstre break the rule**, and they're among the words you'll use most. Luckily Norwegian's irregular group is short — about twenty words — and almost all of them are about family, the body and nature. The full list is on the next page.
**Foreldrene** means "the parents", and the word *foreldre* **only exists in the plural** — there's no *en foreldre*. For one parent, Norwegian simply says *en far* or *ei mor*.

**Én bror with an accent** — *én* (with a mark over the *e*) means "one, just one" and is used when the number is stressed. Without the accent, *en* just means "a". A small difference on paper, a big one in meaning.
**Hvor mange** is for things you can count (*hvor mange katter?*), **hvor mye** for things you can't (*hvor mye kaffe?*) — just like English *how many* and *how much*.

**Katta får barn** — the word *barn* is used for human children **and** young animals, and its plural is exactly the same as its singular: *et barn → to barn*. Its definite plural breaks every rule: *barna*.

grammars.title: The main rule: -er and -ene
body: Four forms, one pattern. This applies to most Norwegian nouns, whatever their gender.
after: Words that already end in *-e* don't double the letter: *en jente* → *jenter*, not *jenteer*.
Words ending in *-el*, *-en*, *-er* drop the middle *e*: *en nøkkel* → *nøkler*, *en søster* → *søstre*, *en vinter* → *vintrer*.
One-syllable words with a single consonant after a short vowel double that consonant: *en venn* → *venner*, *et rom* → *rommer*.

grammars.title: One-syllable neuter nouns: an empty plural
body: One big group you need to recognize right now: **one-syllable *et*-words add nothing in the indefinite plural**. The form is exactly the same as the singular — like English *sheep* or *deer* — and only the number in front tells you.
after: ⚠️ Those with **two** syllables still take *-er*: *et vindu → vinduer*, *et eple → epler*, *et menneske → mennesker*. So the rule isn't "all *et*-words" but "one-syllable *et*-words".
*Barna* is the only real oddity in the last column — its definite plural is *-a*, not *-ene*. Learn it whole; it's a word you'll use every day.

grammars.title: Irregular plurals you must learn
body: This list is short, and everything on it is a common word. Learn it all now, and plurals are done for the whole of A1.
after: Notice the pattern: most of them just **change the vowel** (*bok → bøker*, *mann → menn*, *fot → føtter*). It's a leftover of an old system that English has too — *foot → feet*, *man → men*, *tooth → teeth*. As an English speaker, half this list already feels familiar.
Job titles ending in *-er* have their own tidy pattern: *en lærer → lærere → lærerne*, *en arbeider → arbeidere → arbeiderne*. The plural is just *-e*, and the definite plural *-ne*.

blocks.text: These words come up in almost every getting-to-know-you conversation, and half of them happen to be irregular plurals — so they double as practice for the previous page.

Look at *bestefar* and *bestemor* — literally "best father" and "best mother". Norwegian also has more precise words that tell the two sides of the family apart: *farfar* (father's father), *morfar* (mother's father), *farmor*, *mormor*. English doesn't make this distinction, so it's a genuinely useful extra.

sections.title: Eye training: count as you read

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right. If a row trips you up, underline it and come back to it tomorrow.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Describe your family in four sentences, out loud: how many siblings, where your parents live, how many children are at home, what animals you have.
If you stumble, it's most likely not the plural ending but the **noun's gender** — go back to Unit 4 and rewrite your list with *en/ei/et* in front.
A safe guessing rule: if you don't know a word's plural, use **-er**. You'll be right eight times out of ten, and the rest will still be understood.
The parents live outside the city.
How many cats do they have?
The books are on the table.
